Deliverable 03 · one-page note

Data & methodology

How a snapshot of published facility information became a task-specific comparison tool—and where interpretation must stop.

QuestionCollectionDefinitionsScoringLimitations

Question & users

What space best fits the work?

The primary users are Harvard students choosing among study settings. A second audience is Harvard Library staff deciding which metadata and service improvements would make spaces easier to use. The unit of analysis is one named study space or study area, not a building and not an individual seat.

Collection

103 spaces, 13 libraries, one reproducible snapshot

On 21 September 2026, the project downloaded every record returned by Harvard Library’s public rooms API. It joined each room’s library identifier to the official library metadata API, then checked field labels against the amenity and room-type taxonomies. The resulting CSV contains 103 named spaces across 13 libraries, with 2,098 listed seats.

This is a census of the records returned by the official Find a Space service at that moment—not a sample selected by the project. A small build script cleans HTML from descriptions, maps the three noise codes (0 Silent, 1 Whispers, 2 Chatter), expands 19 amenities into binary columns, and exports CSV, JSON, and the dashboard data file. No personal or sensitive data was collected.

Important coding rule: a 1 means the feature was explicitly listed in the official room record. A 0 means “not listed in that record,” not “the feature definitely does not exist.”

Units & definitions

43 analysis-ready variables

Field groupUnitDefinition
Identity & locationText / coordinatesSpace ID, name, library ID, library, school or unit, floor, address, latitude, and longitude.
Type & capacityCategory / seatsOne of six official room types and the published number of seats. One record has no seat value.
Noise level0, 1, or 2Official space-finder codes: 0 Silent, 1 Whispers, 2 Chatter.
Availability fields0 or 1 / URLReservable flag, open-space flag, booking URL, contact availability, and snapshot library hours.
19 amenity fields0 or 1Accessibility, charging, café, conversation area, couches, food, lockers, media studio, printers, private desks, display, quiet area, reservable amenity, restroom, special collections, standing desks, tech loan, webcam, and whiteboard.
ProvenanceText / dateRoom source URL, library URL, and access date for auditability.
Fit score0–100 pointsWeighted sum of published fields for the selected task; calculated in the browser, not stored as an observed rating.

Scoring

Ratings are task-specific, not popularity ratings

Fit score = sum of the selected goal’s weights when a record has the corresponding published field.

Deep focus gives 30 points to Silent status (20 for Silent plus 10 for Silent-or-Whispers), 20 to private desks, and the remaining 50 to charging, reservability, accessibility, independent/carrel type, standing desks, and the quiet-study amenity. Group work emphasizes collaborative room type, whiteboards, display, reservability, charging, accessibility, six-plus seats, and webcam. Make & present emphasizes media/presentation type, display, tech loan, webcam, whiteboard, and supporting access fields. Comfort break emphasizes soft seating, food/café, charging, accessibility, open-space type, conversation areas, and 20-plus seats.

Each goal’s weights sum to 100. The choices are explicit and reproducible, but they do not represent Harvard policy or surveyed student preferences.

Missing data, bias & uncertainty

What could change the result

  • Coverage boundary: this is complete for the API response, not for every Harvard facility. Classrooms, residential spaces, cafés, outdoor areas, and study places absent from the directory are outside scope.
  • Documentation bias: libraries that publish richer room records can score better even when another space has the same unlisted amenity.
  • No demand data: the dataset has designed capacity but no occupancy, wait times, turnaways, or reservation usage, so it cannot identify crowding.
  • No satisfaction data: the fit score is a model, not a student rating. No survey responses were collected.
  • Access ambiguity: building eligibility, special-collection rules, room hours, and booking requirements vary; the presence of a record does not mean every student can enter at every time.
  • Time sensitivity: hours, equipment, and construction conditions can change; users should check the live source before visiting.
  • Value judgment: weights encode one interpretation of each goal. Light, temperature, proximity, safety perceptions, and atmosphere are not measured.

The dashboard supports facility comparison, metadata auditing, and prioritizing the next questions. It cannot prove that one space is objectively best or that an investment will improve wellbeing or academic outcomes.
